### Problem: Books Exchange (hard version) {#sec-idx-p3-books}

::: {.p-statement}
There are $n$ kids, each holding their own book, and a permutation $p$ of $1..n$. At the end of every day, kid $i$ hands the book they hold to kid $p_i$. For every $i$, print the first day on which kid $i$'s own book comes back to kid $i$. Constraints: $q \le 1000$ queries, $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, sum of $n$ at most $2 \cdot 10^5$. Samples: $p = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] \to [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]$; $[2, 3, 1] \to [3, 3, 3]$; $[4, 6, 2, 1, 5, 3] \to [2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3]$; $[5, 1, 2, 4, 3] \to [4, 4, 4, 1, 4]$.

Source: [CF 1249B2 · Books Exchange (hard version)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1249/B2){.solved rating="1300"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Kid $i$'s book travels $i \to p_i \to p_{p_i} \to \cdots$, so it returns after exactly the length of $i$'s cycle in $p$. Every kid on one cycle gets the same answer, so walk each cycle once, count its length, and write that length into all of its members: $O(n)$ in total.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Follow each book.** For every $i$, walk $j = p_i, p_{p_i}, \ldots$ until $j = i$ and count the steps. Correct (the walk must return, because $p$ is a bijection and so its functional graph is a union of cycles), but a single $n$-cycle makes it $n$ walks of length $n$: $O(n^2)$, too slow for $2 \cdot 10^5$.
2. **One walk per cycle.** Keep `ans[i] = 0` for "not yet known". Scan $i$ left to right; when `ans[i] = 0`, walk the cycle from $i$, collect its members, and write the cycle length into each of them. A later start inside a finished cycle sees `ans` already set and skips it. Each index is walked exactly once.

**Invariant.** After processing start $s$, every index on a cycle that contains some start $\le s$ has its final answer, and no other index has been touched. So each cycle is walked by its smallest member, and only once.
:::

::: {#fig-idx-p3-books}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    perm = [4, 6, 2, 1, 5, 3]
    seen, cycles = [False] * 6, []
    for s in range(6):
        if not seen[s]:
            c, j = [], s
            while not seen[j]:
                seen[j] = True
                c.append(j)
                j = perm[j] - 1
            cycles.append(c)
    assert [len(c) for c in cycles] == [2, 3, 1]
    colors = ["indigo", "green", "amber"]
    owner = {j: colors[k] for k, c in enumerate(cycles) for j in c}
    V.array(ax, p, perm, label="p", colors=owner)
    for i in range(6):
        j = perm[i] - 1
        if j != i:
            V.arrow(ax, p, i + 0.5, -0.1, j + 0.5, -0.1, color=owner[i], rad=0.5 if j > i else -0.5)
    length = {j: len(c) for c in cycles for j in c}
    V.array(ax, p, [length[i] for i in range(6)], x=0.0, y=-3.4, label="ans", colors=owner, index=False)
V.show(draw)
```

The third sample, $p = [4, 6, 2, 1, 5, 3]$ (cells are 0-based, values 1-based). The arrows under the top row join kid $i$ to kid $p_i$. Indigo is the cycle $1 \to 4 \to 1$, green is $2 \to 6 \to 3 \to 2$, and amber is the fixed point $5$. Every kid's answer is the length of their colour class: $[2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3]$.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Follow each book

::: {.form-next}
Simulate one book at a time until it comes home. The walk from $i$ costs the length of $i$'s cycle, so the total is the sum of squared cycle lengths: $O(n^2)$ for one long cycle.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def books_brute(p):
    n = len(p)
    ans = []
    for i in range(n):
        j, days = p[i] - 1, 1
        while j != i:
            j = p[j] - 1
            days += 1
        ans.append(days)
    return ans


assert books_brute([2, 3, 1]) == [3, 3, 3]
assert books_brute([4, 6, 2, 1, 5, 3]) == [2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3]
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> booksBrute(const vector<int>& p) {
    int n = (int)p.size();
    vector<int> ans(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int j = p[i] - 1, days = 1;
        while (j != i) { j = p[j] - 1; days++; }
        ans[i] = days;
    }
    return ans;
}
```

:::

#### One walk per cycle

::: {.form-next}
Walk each cycle once, from its first unvisited member, and write its length into every member. A start whose answer is already known is skipped. Every index is stepped on once: $O(n)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("books", "walk")
    assert str(final) == "[2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def books(p):
    n = len(p)
    ans = [0] * n
    for s in range(n):
        if ans[s]:
            continue                    # s lies on a cycle already measured
        cycle, j = [], s
        while True:
            cycle.append(j)
            j = p[j] - 1
            if j == s:
                break
        for u in cycle:
            ans[u] = len(cycle)
    return ans


assert books([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
assert books([2, 3, 1]) == [3, 3, 3]
assert books([4, 6, 2, 1, 5, 3]) == [2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3]       # the board sample
assert books([1]) == [1]
assert books([3, 4, 1, 2]) == [2, 2, 2, 2]
assert books([5, 1, 2, 4, 3]) == [4, 4, 4, 1, 4]
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 15)
    p = random.sample(range(1, n + 1), n)
    assert books(p) == books_brute(p)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int q;
    scanf("%d", &q);
    while (q--) {
        int n;
        scanf("%d", &n);
        vector<int> p(n), ans(n, 0), cycle;
        for (int& x : p) { scanf("%d", &x); x--; }
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {
            if (ans[s]) continue;
            cycle.clear();
            int j = s;
            do { cycle.push_back(j); j = p[j]; } while (j != s);
            for (int u : cycle) ans[u] = (int)cycle.size();
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%d ", ans[i]);
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Follow each book:** $O(\sum_C |C|^2)$ over the cycles $C$, which is $O(n^2)$ in the worst case; $O(1)$ extra. **One walk per cycle:** $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the answers and one cycle buffer.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Fixed point ($p_i = i$): the book is handed to oneself and is back after day $1$; the answer is $1$, not $0$.
- One big cycle: every answer is $n$, and the brute force does $n^2$ steps; this is the test that separates the forms.
- 1-based input: convert once (`x--` in C++); mixing bases inside the walk sends it to the wrong kid or past the end of the array.
- The easy version (B1, $n \le 200$) accepts the brute force; the hard version needs the per-cycle walk.
:::
